output.brief: The jump in write-offs is mainly an inside-the-DC problem, not a Haverlow problem. After night receiving was cut from six to four operatives in late July, the median time from unloading to reaching a chilled chamber rose from about 44 minutes to nearly 4 hours on nights. Dock staging areas are unrefrigerated and ran 15–17°C overnight. Haverlow product measured 2.4–3.5°C on the trailer when doors opened, with no reefer alarms and no trend. The warm receipt probe readings are taken hours later, after the product has sat on the dock. Night write-offs rose from 0.6% to 2.9% for every supplier, and day-shift rates barely moved. The chambers held temperature. Don't raise the chargeback or move volume: it would punish the wrong party. Restore the night team to six, set and monitor a maximum dock-to-chamber time, and keep the receiving probe. Separately, pull Corriebank's claim-level data to test whether the roughly £1,850/week rise in its credits includes over-claiming. That part is unproven, and the timing alone doesn't establish it. I'm fairly confident in the main finding. The customer-credit question remains open.
